issues.legal_issue: A High Court may decide an unresolved title issue in a second appeal when the first appellate court did not determine title and instead disposed of the appeal on an unsupported finding.
material_facts: The first appellate court dismissed the appeal on the basis that the purchaser was a bona fide purchaser, without making a finding on title.
The bona fide purchaser finding was unsupported by evidence and did not address the applicable legal principles.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to decide the title issue because the first appellate court had left it open; its intervention did not amount to setting aside concurrent findings on title.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 100 and 101 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appeal is not ordinarily an occasion to reappraise concurrent findings of fact. But where the first appellate court has not decided the relevant title issue, the High Court may decide that open issue. A finding unsupported by evidence and reached without applying the governing legal principles does not bind the High Court. The judgment refers to the established rule against disturbing factual findings in second appeal, tracing it to a Privy Council ruling and noting its acceptance by this Court, but gives no case names.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from a first appellate decision.
predicates.first_appellate_court_left_title_undecid: The first appellate court disposed of the appeal without deciding the title issue.

issues.definition: When a second appeal concerns title that the first appellate court left undecided, the High Court may decide that unresolved title issue.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee invoking the protection for a transfer by an ostensible owner must prove the conditions for that protection, and a transferee who knows that the transferor's title is defective cannot establish good faith.
material_facts: The purchaser and transferor belonged to the same village.
The transferor sold the land on the day he was required to appear before revenue authorities considering a challenge to the recorded ownership.
Although the sale deed was executed earlier, the purchaser paid most of the consideration three years later.
The purchaser obtained an indemnity bond from the transferor against loss concerning the land.
These circumstances showed that the purchaser knew the transferor's title was disputed and took a risk in purchasing the land.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was not a bona fide purchaser in good faith and could not rely on the ostensible-owner exception to establish title to the whole property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act is an exception to the general rule that a person cannot transfer a better title than that person possesses. The transferee bears the burden of proving that the transferor was the ostensible owner with the consent of the persons interested in the property, and that the transferee took reasonable care to ascertain the transferor's power to transfer and acted in good faith. Knowledge that the transferor's title is disputed is inconsistent with good faith.

predicates.ostensible_owner_protection_claimed: A transferee seeks protection for a transfer made by someone who appeared to be the owner.
predicates.transferee_knew_transferor_title_was_def: The transferee knew that the transferor's title was disputed or defective when acquiring the property.

issues.definition: If a transferee seeks protection for a transfer by an apparent owner and knew that the transferor's title was disputed or defective, the transferee is not entitled to that protection.

issues.legal_issue: A substituted revenue entry supported by facts proved before the revenue authorities is presumed correct unless the party challenging it proves otherwise.
material_facts: The original revenue entry incorrectly recorded the whole land in the name of one co-sharer, although the co-sharers' partition allocated shares of one-eighth and seven-eighths.
A corrected entry was made following an inquiry by a subordinate revenue officer whose report and annexures recited the partition and the co-sharers' application for mutation.
The transferor's admission occurred after he had transferred his interest and could not by itself bind the purchaser.
The purchaser adduced no evidence to rebut the presumption arising from the corrected entry.
issues.conclusion: The corrected entry was made in accordance with facts proved before the revenue authorities, was presumed correct, and was not rebutted by the purchaser.
issues.legal_principle: Section 37(a) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 permits entries to be made in accordance with facts proved or admitted to have occurred. Under section 44, an entry made in accordance with the law is presumed true until the contrary is proved or a new entry is lawfully substituted. Although an admission by a person made after parting with an interest cannot itself bind a purchaser, other evidence proving the relevant facts may support the entry and give rise to the presumption.

predicates.corrected_revenue_entry_disputed: A party disputes the correctness of a substituted entry in a revenue record.
predicates.substituted_entry_supported_by_facts_pro: The substituted entry was made on the basis of facts proved before the authorities responsible for the record.
predicates.challenger_adduced_no_rebuttal_evidence: The party challenging the entry presented no evidence sufficient to disprove it.

issues.definition: When a disputed substituted revenue entry is supported by facts proved before the responsible authorities and the challenger presents no rebuttal evidence, the entry is presumed true.
